note: Short excerpts from public guidance pages, kept for the essay reviewer's guidance (guidance.md). Fair use: at most 300 words per source, cited by organization and url. No student essays. Refresh: npm run research-essay-guidance.

sources.title: Run On Sentences
excerpts: Run-ons, comma splices, and fused sentences are all names given to compound sentences that are not punctuated correctly.
Join the two independent clauses with one of the coordinating conjunctions (and, but, for, or, nor, so, yet), and use a comma before the connecting word.
When you do not have a connecting word (or when you use a connecting word other than and, but, for, or nor, so, or yet between the two independent clauses) use a semicolon (;).
So, run-ons and fused sentences are terms describing two independent clauses that are joined together with no connecting word or punctuation to separate the clauses.

sources.title: Extended Rules for Commas
excerpts: Use commas to separate independent clauses when they are joined by any of these seven coordinating conjunctions: and, but, for, or, nor, so, yet.
Use commas after introductory a) clauses, b) phrases, or c) words that come before the main clause.
Use a pair of commas in the middle of a sentence to set off clauses, phrases, and words that are not essential to the meaning of the sentence.

sources.title: Concision
excerpts: The goal of concise writing is to use the most effective words.
Concise writing does not always have the fewest words, but it always uses the strongest ones.
Words and phrases should be deliberately chosen for the work they are doing.
As a general rule, more specific words lead to more concise writing.
Check every word to make sure that it is providing something important and unique to a sentence.

sources.title: Sentence Clarity
excerpts: Avoid interrupting the main clause with a phrase or subordinate clause if the interruption will cause confusion.
Sentences in active voice are usually easier to understand than those in passive voice because active-voice constructions indicate clearly the performer of the action expressed in the verb.
When you have a series of words, phrases, or clauses, put them in parallel form (similar grammatical construction) so that the reader can identify the linking relationship more easily and clearly.
Use verbs when possible rather than noun forms known as " nominalizations ."
Use affirmative forms rather than several negatives because multiple negatives are difficult to understand.

sources.title: Advice for Writing Application Essays
excerpts: Don't use boilerplate essays.
That is, resist the urge to reuse the exact same essay for different schools if each of them is giving you a slightly different writing prompt.
You can, of course, adapt the same essay for similar prompts.
Before you can start writing your essay, you will need to begin by reading the prompts and questions carefully.
Just make sure that you eventually come to have a rough draft that is about one thing.
After reading your essay, does it seem like anyone could have written this?
Successful essays relate an experience or analyze a pattern from the writer’s life.

It is not enough to make general claims about what impacted your decision to go to college, for instance; you must elaborate by including evidence that answers “how” and “why” when you make your claims.

That is not meant to add an extra layer of anxiety to your writing process, but to highlight the fact that you don’t necessarily need to have something life-changing to write about in order to write a successful essay.
Ask yourself if the essay answers the prompt.
As you are drafting and revising, feel free to fix any mistakes that you catch in terms of spelling, grammar, and mechanics, but don’t spend too much time editing early on in the writing process.
Working on lower-order concerns can give you the impression that the essay is ready to submit prematurely.

sources.title: Admissions Application Essay: Writing your Way to College (handout)
excerpts: You want to use your essay to quickly capture their attention and provide them with new information that is not readily found elsewhere on your application in a clear and concise manner.

While we know you have many accomplishments to talk about, talking about too many things with such a limited word count will inevitably make your discussions more surface-level and detract from your essay.
Don’t tell them you’re resourceful, show them how you’ve developed and demonstrated that trait.
While you may have many guest stars in your paper and be super thankful to your band teacher, make sure you are highlighting your special skills and unique attributes.
Gimmicks, cliches, and humor are all risks.
Think about the structure of the paper including the overall theme, introduction, the body paragraphs, and how you’re going to purposefully use your conclusion to do more than summarize.

sources.title: The Personal Statement
excerpts: What details of your life (personal or family problems, history, people or events that have shaped you or influenced your goals) might help the committee better understand you or help set you apart from other applicants?
Don't be tempted to use the same statement for all applications.
In every case, be sure your answer fits the question being asked.
Think in terms of showing or demonstrating through concrete experience.
Don't, for example, state that you would make an excellent doctor unless you can back it up with specific reasons.
The lead or opening paragraph is generally the most important.

sources.title: Steps for Revising
excerpts: Read your paper out loud and listen for awkward pauses and unclear ideas.
Cut out extra words, vagueness, and misused words.
If you think something is wrong, you should make a note of it, even if you don't know how to fix it.
Try to detach yourself from what you've written; pretend that you are reviewing someone else's work.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Fragments and Run-ons
excerpts: A sentence fragment is an incomplete sentence.
Finally, you need to know that every dependent clause needs to be attached to an independent clause (remember, the independent clause can stand on its own).
You are making a run-on when you put two complete sentences (a subject and its predicate and another subject and its predicate) together in one sentence without separating them properly.
NOTE : You CANNOT simply add a comma between the two sentences, or you’ll end up with what’s called a “ comma splice .”
You can fix a comma splice the same way you fix a run-on—either change the punctuation or add a conjunction.
The good news is that writers tend to be either comma splicers or run-on artists, but almost never both.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Commas
excerpts: Read what comes after FANBOYS all by itself.
If you don’t have FANBOYS between the two complete and separate thoughts, using a comma alone causes a “comma splice” or “fused sentence” (some instructors may call it a run-on).
Some readers (especially professors) will think of this as a serious error.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Application Essays
excerpts: One of the basic tasks of the application essay is to follow the directions.
Make sure you follow page and word limits exactly—err on the side of shortness, not length.
Find the most relevant, memorable, concrete statements and focus in on them.

Eliminate any generalizations or platitudes (“I’m a people person”, “Doctors save lives”, or “Mr. Calleson’s classes changed my life”), or anything that could be cut and pasted into anyone else’s application.

Eliminate irrelevant issues (“I was a track star in high school, so I think I’ll make a good veterinarian.”) or issues that might be controversial for your reader (“My faith is the one true faith, and only nurses with that faith are worthwhile,” or “Lawyers who only care about money are evil.”).
Just make sure that you replace the generalizations with examples as you revise.
A hint: you may find yourself writing a good, specific sentence right after a general, meaningless one.
Applications that have several short-answer essays require even more detail.
Get straight to the point in every case, and address what they’ve asked you to address.
Do address any information about yourself and your application that needs to be explained (for example, weak grades or unusual coursework for your program).
Don’t waste space with information you have provided in the rest of the application.
The voice you use in your essay should be yours.
BUT be careful not to let your drama turn into melodrama.
Don’t invent drama where there isn’t any, and don’t let the drama take over.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Introductions
excerpts: Try writing your introduction last.
Essentially, this kind of weaker introduction contains several sentences that are vague and don’t really say much.
Restating the question can sometimes be an effective strategy, but it can be easy to stop at JUST restating the question instead of offering a more specific, interesting introduction to your paper.

This kind of introduction generally makes broad, sweeping statements about the relevance of this topic since the beginning of time, throughout the world, etc. It is usually very general (similar to the placeholder introduction) and fails to connect to the thesis.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Conclusions
excerpts: You can also use this strategy on your own, asking yourself “So What?” as you develop your ideas or your draft.
Include a brief summary of the paper’s main points, but don’t simply repeat things that were in your paper.
This conclusion just restates the thesis and is usually painfully short.
It does not push the ideas forward.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Paragraphs
excerpts: Paragraphs are the building blocks of papers.
Ultimately, a paragraph is a sentence or group of sentences that support one main idea.
Unified : All of the sentences in a single paragraph should be related to a single controlling idea (often expressed in the topic sentence of the paragraph).

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Word Choice
excerpts: The main way to avoid clichés is first to recognize them and then to create shorter, fresher equivalents.
In contrast, if you find yourself frustrated, tiredly repeating the same nouns, verbs, or adjectives, or making the same point over and over, you are probably being redundant.
Be careful when using the thesaurus.
Don’t try to impress your reader or sound unduly authoritative.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Style
excerpts: First, remember that your goal in academic writing is not to sound intelligent, but to get your intelligent point across.
And don’t blindly accept the recommendations of your word processing program’s thesaurus—these tools may be dangerous unless you double-check the meaning of the words in a dictionary.
In fact, it’s often okay to repeat the same word(s) in your paper, particularly when they are significant or central terms.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Writing Concisely
excerpts: Common examples of redundant pairs include: full and complete, each and every, hopes and dreams, whole entire, first and foremost, true and accurate, always and forever.
“In the event that” and “under circumstances in which” can be replaced with if.”It is necessary that” and “cannot be avoided” can be replaced with must or should.

sources.title: Editing and Proofreading
excerpts: When you’ve worked hard to develop and present your ideas, you don’t want careless errors distracting your reader from what you have to say.
Try to keep the editing and proofreading processes separate.
Don’t rely entirely on spelling checkers.
In addition, spell checkers will not catch misspellings that form another valid word.
Read the paper backwards.

sources.organization: The Writing Center, University of Wisconsin–Madison
sources.title: Use the active voice
excerpts: Generally, try to use the active voice whenever possible.
Passive voice sentences often use more words, can be vague, and can lead to a tangle of prepositional phrases.
There are sometimes good reasons to use the passive voice.

excerpts: But remember: when you narrate your life story, you will reflect on what you have learned from those experiences.

For this, it is key to familiarize yourself with the program’s website: their mission, faculty, courses, values, opportunities, etc. Identify keywords you might use when narrating and evaluating your past experiences.

sources.title: Comma Splices, Run-ons, & Sentence Fragments
excerpts: A comma splice occurs when two sentences or independent clauses are joined together by a comma, while a run-on sentence occurs when two sentences or independent clauses are joined without proper punctuation.
Sentences or independent clauses must be separated by punctuation other than a comma or by a comma with a coordinating conjunction ( for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so ).
Both comma splices and run-ons are fixed using the same methods.

sources.title: Run-Ons and Comma Splices (handout)
excerpts: A run-on sentence occurs when two independent clauses are mistakenly combined into one sentence without any punctuation.
Note that this means that a sentence can become a run-on if it has a coordinating conjunction but no comma.
The sentence doesn't have to be long to be a run-on.
If the two thoughts are not very closely tied together, then use a period instead.

excerpts: The word limits for these essays often land at less than 300 words (except for the Personal Statement), so while you may be used to writing more than that for school, you will need to practice dialing it back and being a bit more concise for these essays.

excerpts: While the essay is a valuable tool that we use to understand you better, it is rarely if ever a “make or break” component of your application.

If you ask too many people for feedback, you’ll end up incorporating so many extensive and varied edits that your final product will no longer sound like you, but like a junk sculpture composed of a gazillion voices that all sound different rather than your own strong and confident voice.
Finally, don’t obsess over any one word or sentence.
